headline: Hidden Population of Rare Lorises Found in China's Forests
meta_description: Scientists documented 98 northern pygmy slow lorises in Guangxi, China, doubling the country's known population of this endangered primate species.
summary_short: A recent study in Guangxi, China found 98 northern pygmy slow lorises—nearly doubling the country's known population of this endangered species.
body:
Researchers surveying the rugged karst forests of Guangxi, China, have made a striking discovery: 98 northern pygmy slow lorises living in the wild, a finding that roughly doubles the country's previously known population of the endangered primates. Published in the journal Integrative Zoology by scientists at Guangxi Normal University, the study suggests that a substantial population of these nocturnal creatures had simply gone undetected. The northern pygmy slow loris, scientifically named Xanthonycticebus intermedius, was only recognized as a distinct species in 2023, after genetic research separated it from its southern relative. These animals are plumper, fuzzier, and possess a flatter "button nose" compared to their close kin—characteristics that unfortunately make them more desirable in the illegal wildlife trade.

The research team surveyed six areas between June and October 2025, covering nearly 286 kilometers across Guangxi. They found lorises in four of the six locations, with the highest concentration of 37 individuals in Longzhou. What makes this discovery particularly significant is that 79 of the 98 lorises documented were living outside protected areas, leaving them vulnerable to hunting and capture for the pet and traditional medicine trades. Anna Nekaris, a conservation professor at Anglia Ruskin University, emphasized that the animals' elusive nocturnal habits had simply meant nobody was looking for them in Guangxi until now.

The finding offers cautious hope for the species, though challenges remain. While slow lorises can survive in fragmented forests where food remains available, their perceived cuteness makes them prime targets for traders. The animals are the world's only venomous primates, routinely defanged before sale as pets—a procedure that also removes their toothcomb, essential for grooming and feeding. Protecting these newly discovered populations will require urgent conservation efforts and stronger enforcement against wildlife trafficking.
quick_facts: 98 northern pygmy slow lorises documented in Guangxi, China in 2025
Species only recognized as distinct in 2023 after genetic research
79 of 98 lorises found outside protected areas, facing wildlife trade threats
Highest concentration: 37 individuals in Longzhou, Guangxi
